summary:
Arequipa department has no region-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding on record. The attached sources are national in scope and, as national measures, bind the department, so the operative legal frame for a visitor to Arequipa is Peru's.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The facility restriction is in force. On 20 February 2025 the Congress commission on women and family unanimously approved a dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457 that would bar entry to public sanitary facilities destined to the sex opposite to one's birth sex, with exceptions for custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and would require unambiguous signage; at that date the measure still awaited plenary backing. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho called it discriminatory and warned that security staff would effectively judge people by personal criteria, such as requesting their DNI.

The Congress plenary approved the governing statute on 2 April 2025, exempt from second vote: the law strengthening the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents. Its article 5 bars anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex from public sanitary facilities, with exceptions limited to accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. IDEHPUCP analysts Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte find that the provision implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable biological sex, and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination. They note that Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage.

The same April 2025 legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Its vague child-protection articles, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. IDEHPUCP also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard the domestic facility restriction does not meet.

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private as well as public life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report records 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women the most affected and hate crimes rising. Its 2024 co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The report recounts the February 2023 kidnapping of trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her murder in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang, the bodies showing gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting that indicate extreme hate.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

The 2017 repeal of LGBT coverage from the Penal Code, carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members after an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition claiming one million signatures, leaves Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking such coverage.

A regional standard runs against the domestic restriction. Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights holds that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The December 2025 sentencing of Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León to 17 years for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín reached that Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and, per BBC News Mundo, stands as the Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.

Recorded violence figures understate the risk environment. The TLGBI Rights Observatory logged 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023, and co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that these figures are only a sub-registry. The February 2023 killing of Rubí Torres Silvano, shot approximately 30 times by the 'Los Gallegos' gang after her kidnapping in central Lima, is presented in the report as evidence of extreme hate rather than ordinary homicide.

Two developments cut the other way. In June 2024 health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court struck down an anti-equality decree after an activist legal challenge. Neither reverses the facility restriction or restores hate-crime coverage.

Speech and association are constrained alongside facilities. localsOnly:
Security staff at public facilities apply the restriction on their own judgment. Gianna Camacho warned that staff would effectively assess people by personal criteria such as requesting a DNI, which places the decision at the door rather than with any authority.

Recourse against private enforcement has failed at least once. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that applied the policy, so residents challenging exclusion by private venues should not expect that body to intervene.

Residents face limits on public messaging and on media content. The April 2025 package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity', and its article 4 restricts media and advertising content, with the minimum obscenity sentence raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Congress has treated trans people as a legitimate object of hostile speech. IDEHPUCP recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu, and Congress has again rejected equal marriage while banning inclusive language.

Healthcare settings improved on terminology. In June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terms for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients.

Public figures are targeted for harassment over facilities. Presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, to 'go use the men's room'.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Arequipa-specific incident data, municipal ordinance, regional government directive or police instruction on facility access appears in the sources. Whether any local authority has issued implementing rules for the April 2025 law is unresolved and not sourced here.

The sources do not state whether the July 2025 constitutional court ruling against an anti-equality decree bears on the facility provision or on the article 4 content restrictions. The scope of that ruling is unresolved.

National hate-crime and killing figures for 2020 to 2023 are not broken down by department in the sources, so the share of recorded violence occurring in Arequipa is not sourced. Gianna Camacho's statement that the figures are a sub-registry means the true count is higher, by an amount the sources do not quantify.

Whether the 2024 removal of pathologising terminology from health guidance has been implemented in Arequipa's healthcare facilities is not documented in the sources.

The sources do not record how often security staff in Arequipa have demanded identity documents or refused entry under article 5, so the practical frequency of the restriction in the department remains unresolved.
